title: Greedy: Partition Labels
oneLiner: Cut a string into as many pieces as possible so each letter lives in one piece: record each letter's last index, then close a piece when you reach the furthest last index seen.
keyTakeaway: A piece that contains a letter must stretch to that letter's LAST occurrence. So store last[c] for every letter, then scan: end = max(end, last[s[i]]). When i == end, nothing inside the piece appears later, so cut there. Cutting as early as possible is what makes the piece count as large as possible: O(n) time, O(1) space for a fixed 26-letter alphabet.
explanation:
Split a string of lowercase letters into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part, and return the length of each part in order. For "ababcbacadefegdehijhklij" the answer is [9, 7, 8]: "ababcbaca", "defegde", "hijhklij". Joining the parts back together must give the original string, so you're choosing where to cut, not rearranging.

Think about the first part. It starts at index 0, so it contains s[0], so it must reach at least the last occurrence of s[0]. Every letter inside that stretch drags the end further, to its own last occurrence. Once the scan reaches the current end and nothing has pushed it further, the part is self-contained, and cutting right there is the earliest legal cut. Cutting as early as possible is safe (and so greedy works) because an earlier cut never forces a later one to move: the rest of the string has exactly the same constraints either way, so it can be split just as finely.

Two passes. First, last[c] = the final index of each letter (an int[26] in C#, or a dict in Python). Second, scan with start = 0 and end = 0: at each i set end = max(end, last[s[i]]); when i == end, append end - start + 1 and set start = i + 1. Both passes are O(n). The extra space is 26 counters no matter how long the string is, which counts as O(1).

In C#, s[i] - 'a' turns a char into 0 to 25 (a char subtracts as a number). In Python, use ord(ch) - ord('a'), or just key a dict by the character.

The visualization scans "abacdcbe": the highlighted cells are the current part and the tracker is end.

recognitionSignals: "Each character / value appears in at most one part" with parts kept in their original order.
The answer depends on the first and last position of each item: precompute last occurrences.
Maximise the number of parts, so cut as early as is legal.
gotchas: end only grows: use max(end, last[s[i]]), never assign last[s[i]] directly.
The part length is end - start + 1, and the next part starts at i + 1.
Sorting or rearranging the letters changes the problem; the parts must stay contiguous and in order.
confusableWith: Merge Intervals: each letter defines an interval [first, last], and the parts are exactly the merged intervals. This lesson gets them in one pass without building or sorting intervals.
Sliding Window: both scan with a moving boundary, but a window shrinks from the left; here a part only grows until it closes for good.

complexity.note: Two linear passes: record each letter's last index, then scan and cut. The table has 26 entries whatever the length, so extra space is constant (the output list aside).
